Rule 1 satisfied: 27 passing, clean typecheck.

**Naming evaluation (first priority)** — I walked every identifier. The premium side is well-named and the domain vocabulary is consistent. Two candidates:

- `damagedItem(policy, damage)` — reads as a noun returning the item, accurate. Keep.
- `consumeCap(policy, result)` — its comment says the split is deliberate. Keep.
- `runStep`'s `precedingContracts` vs `runScenario`'s `contractsSoFar` — same value, two names across a one-hop call. Minor, but it's a real intent wobble.

The one genuine finding is a **Rule 3 (duplication) / Rule 2 (intent)** issue that the naming pass surfaced:

`basePremiumForType` and `insuranceValueForType` are the same shape: lookup a `string` in an `InsurableItemType`-keyed table via an unchecked cast. The cast is duplicated conceptual knowledge — "item types are validated elsewhere" — stated twice.

But extracting a shared `lookupByType(table, type)` helper would need a generic to preserve the two tables' distinct literal types, and would push the two well-named call sites behind a generic indirection. That trades Rule 2 clarity for a Rule 3 win of two lines. Rule 2 trumps Rule 3. Not worth it.

Let me check the actual APP asymmetry I found instead — `sumBasePremiums`/`sumItemSurcharges`/`insuranceSumFor` are three reducers over `Item[]`, all `(total, x) => total + f(x)`:

Four `reduce`-to-a-sum sites with three different accumulator names (`total`, `total`, `sum`, `total`). This is the strongest Rule 3 + Rule 2 finding: one concept (sum a mapped list) written four ways. A `sumBy` helper collapses all four.

Let me measure the APP mass of that change before committing to it.

**Current mass, the four reducer sites:**

| Site | constants | bindings | invocations | loops | mass |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sumBasePremiums` (l.93-96) | 1 (`0`) | 3 (`items`,`total`,`group`) | 3 (`intoAlikeGroups`,`basePremiumForGroup`,`+`) = 6 | 1 (`reduce`) = 5 | 15 |
| `sumItemSurcharges` (l.117) | 1 | 3 | 2 (`surchargeForItem`,`+`) = 4 | 5 | 13 |
| `insuranceSumFor` (l.196) | 1 | 3 | 2 (`insuranceValueForType`,`+`) = 4 | 5 | 13 |
| `settleClaim` payout (l.236-239) | 1 | 3 | 2 (`payoutForDamage`,`+`) = 4 | 5 | 13 |

Total: **54**.

With a `sumBy` helper the four loops collapse to one (5 instead of 20), but each call site gains an invocation and keeps its lambda. Estimated after: helper ~13, plus four sites at ~7 each = **41**. A real reduction of 13.

However — the four lambdas differ in what they map over: `AlikeGroup[]`, `Item[]`, `Item[]`, `Damage[]`. A generic `sumBy<T>(xs: T[], f: (x: T) => number)` handles that, but each call site becomes `sumBy(items, surchargeForItem)` — which is arguably *clearer* than the explicit reduce. Let me apply it.

content.text: All 27 green, typecheck clean. Let me verify the final state of the changed regions.

Refactoring complete. All 27 tests green, `tsc --noEmit` clean.

## Naming evaluation (first priority)

Walked every identifier. The domain vocabulary is consistent and the premium-side names read well. Three candidates considered and rejected:

- `damagedItem` — reads as a noun returning the item; accurate. Keep.
- `consumeCap` — the existing comment documents why it is deliberately split from `settleClaim`. Keep.
- `precedingContracts` (in `runStep`) vs `contractsSoFar` (in `runScenario`) — the same value under two names across a one-hop call. A real but minor wobble; renaming touches a signature for no behavioural clarity gain, so I left it. Worth noting as a future cleanup.

## Refactoring applied — Rule 3 (duplication), reinforcing Rule 2

Four `reduce`-to-a-sum sites expressed one concept ("sum a mapped list") four different ways, with three different accumulator names (`total`, `total`, `sum`, `total`). Extracted a single generic helper in `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-04_06-20-44_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.1.1-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking-2/src/claim-office.ts`:

```ts
const sumBy = <T>(items: T[], amountOf: (item: T) => number): number =>
  items.reduce((total, item) => total + amountOf(item), 0);
```

Applied to `sumBasePremiums`, `sumItemSurcharges`, `insuranceSumFor`, and the payout fold in `settleClaim`. Two sites became point-free (`sumBy(items, surchargeForItem)`); the other two keep a lambda because they map `item.type` or close over `policy`. Tests were run after each of the four edits individually — green throughout.

## APP mass

| Site | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `sumBasePremiums` | 15 | 7 |
| `sumItemSurcharges` | 13 | 7 |
| `insuranceSumFor` | 13 | 9 |
| `settleClaim` payout | 13 | 9 |
| `sumBy` helper | — | 13 |
| **Total** | **54** | **45** |

Delta −9. Four loops (mass 5 each) collapsed to one; the helper's own mass and the added invocation at each call site absorb part of the gain.

## Considered and rejected

`basePremiumForType` and `insuranceValueForType` are structurally identical — both cast a `string` into an `InsurableItemType`-keyed table, duplicating the "types are validated elsewhere" assumption. A shared generic lookup would save two lines but push two well-named call sites behind an indirection that obscures which table is being read. Rule 2 trumps Rule 3; left as is.

All constraints from your brief were respected: no dragon-material clause, no folded multiplier, no threshold changes, no rounding/clamping/error handling, `intoAlikeGroups` untouched, both non-null assertions left in place. Note that `sumBy` is a pure structural extraction — it does not alter addition order within any fold, so the IEEE-754 behaviour under `Math.ceil` is bit-identical to before.
